content.summary_of_the_paper: The operator and configuration choices in the neural network model design space have different impacts on INT8 quantization and thus lead to diver quantization efficiency. This work proposes SpaceEvo to efficiently search a quantization-friendly search space. The key idea is to use the average performance of top-tier sub-networks that meet the latency requirements in the search space to measure the quality of the search space. In addition, a block-wise quantized accuracy lookup table is built to reduce the expensive search cost. Experiments show that SpaceEvo achieves 2.1x faster than EfficientNetB0 with 0.9% higher accuracy on Pixel4-A1 CPU.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ detailed experiments and analysis on the relationship between FLOPs, FP32 performance, and INT8 quantization performance on two mobile CPUs. 
+ the proposed quality score (Q-T score) is a good approximate metric of the search space quality.
+ detailed ablation study on Q-T score effectiveness, space search effectiveness, and search cost

Weakness:
- Experiments are mostly done with two mobile CPUs. It is uncertain whether the on-device quantization efficiency analysis in this paper still holds for mobile GPUs and even mobile NPUs or not.
- SpaceEvo requires two stages of search: search of design space and search of neural network in the searched design space. It is unclear the overall search cost compared to other one-stage NAS  approaches in Table 2 and 3.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-organized and easy to follow.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work systematically investigates the quantization effects on the design spaces and proposes a new metric to search the quantization-friendly search space. My major concern is that all experiments are conducted on two mobile CPUs and the effectiveness of SpaceEvo is not evaluated on mobile GPUs. In general, I think this paper is marginally above the acceptance threshold.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents a two-stage NAS process for discovering accurate and quantization-friendly neural networks.
It begins by analysing performance gains from quantizing different operations to INT8 in the context of two target devices (Pixel 4 and Intel VNNI).
It then follows with a design of a large search space (called hyperspace) which is constructed by considering a number of candidate operations (7 different ones, called blocks) and a set of hyperparameters for them (such as different kernel size, output channels, etc., called configurations).
The searching algorithm is then proposed, utilizing a progressive, two-stage approach.
In the first stage, the goal is to find a subset of the original hyperspace that would result, on average, in the best final result after the second stage (standard NAS objective) is run on this subspace.
Different subspaces are obtained by restricting the first-stage search to only consider different selection of blocks and their output channels across different stages of the macro model, while the choice of other hyperparameters (e.g., kernel size) is left for the second-stage search.
The authors further propose to utilise blockwise quantization combined with knowledge distillation (BKD) to speed up the process of assessing each subspace - similarly, for latency constraints, a predictor based on nn-Meter is utilized to efficiently predict on-device latency of each configurations; both are then used together with an evolutionary algorithm to conduct stage 1 search (called space search).
After a good subspace is identified, second-stage search is conducted to find Pareto-optimal architectures by further constructing a supernet, training it in a quantization-aware way, and finally performing constrained search of a subetnet using evolutionary algorithm.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**

 - The paper is well written and easy to follow
 - The proposed method is well motivated and delivers strong empirical results
 - Evaluation present in the paper seems correct and the experimental setting for each method is controlled well (at least most of the time)
 
 **Weaknesses:**
 
 - (W1) When it comes to the proposed searching methodology and implications for the broader NAS research, the paper does not include any significantly novel parts -- pretty much every single element or insights has been already proposed/made (see details), however not necessarily in the context of quantization-friendly NAS; the proposed system _is not_ trivial in the sense that I can imagine putting everything together and achieving strong results was a lot of work, therefore I wouldn't say there is no value in presenting these results, but it seems that the paper presents what I would describe as a very well-engineered proof point that existing state-of-the-art methods can deliver strong performance in the context of quantization-aware NAS. Neither the methodology, nor the results, seem particularly inspiring for future research, considering what can be already found in the literature.
 - Despite combining a lot of methods and steps, the proposed method is not adequately ablated, making it hard to understand how different parts of the system contribute to the overall strong performance. For example, what if we skipped stage 2 altogether and rely on the fact that performing stage 1 already produces some candidate architectures (from Eq. 2)? How much would you say the final accuracy is conditioned on the entire process (e.g., including BKD from EfficientNet-B5)? What if you retrain selected architectures in isolation from random initialisation? More broadly, at what points (if any) resetting weights would have impact on the final performance?
 - reported GPU cost in Table 5 is wrong and it is something I am quite sensitive to as many papers try to appear better through that; the authors report 24 __GPU hours__, which is related to the following sentence: "In our work, the BKD and lookup table construction can be sped up in a parallel way and finished in 1 day, which amounts a one-time cost before the space search". It is **incorrect to report wall-clock time of a parallelized workload as searching cost**. I invite the authors to check the definition of GPU-hour, alternatively they can try to rent 8 GPUs on AWS and check if the final cost is going to be 8 times lower than when using 1 GPU... In short, the **cost** of searching stays the same regardless of how many GPUs we use - this is very important, there is no point in comparing different searching methods though the lenses of how many GPUs their authors can throw at the problem. Although, admittedly, the ability to parallelize things is desired and important, but it is not the same as the cost of running a search.
 - End-to-end searching cost is never reported.
 - The authors really push the boundaries of what is acceptable in terms of squeezing the text... I am not sure if accepting the paper in its current form would be really fair to other submissions that try to respect limits. One of the problems here is that the paper _will have to be cut_ if accepted, as simply including authors information will result in an overflow and there is really no space in the current version to accommodate for that. What are the authors going to remove and how is that not going to significantly affect the paper? And if there is such a thing then why hasn't it be removed before submitting?
 - benchmarking on a single core (Appendix A) seems unjustified and makes me question if any conclusion from latency measurements would be applicable to real-world scenarios, especially in the case of Intel VNNI, which employs a 10 cores/20 threads CPU according to Table 6. I am not sure why the authors decided to benchmark execution using a single core only. The text in Appendix A mentions fairness but I don't see how this is an issue considering that comparing execution times between different devices is not the point of this paper. It also makes me wonder how performance of different models, especially baselines (e.g., Tables 2 and 3), has been affected by this choice.

 
**Minor shortcomings and suggestions:**

 - Analysis presented in Section 2 might be ok as a motivation behind the rest of the paper, but frankly it does not stand on its own and the authors should probably make it clear that it merely suggests certain situations can exist, rather than presenting them as some significant, generic insights. For example, FP32 vs. INT8 is presented by considering two models on a single device - what is more, no attempt has been made to explain why we observe the behaviour, resulting in easily questionable foundation for drawing any conclusion. Yet, the paper quite clearly concludes that: "FP32 latency [is a] bad indicator of INT8 latency" in Observation 1. Formally speaking, the results are insufficient to draw this particular conclusion. Please iron out details like.
 - Similarly, in Appendix B, Figure 9 shows interesting latency behaviour for #channels between 624 and 672. But according to Figure 4 the largest number of channels considered in this work is 448. Is the Figure in the Appendix really relevant for the rest of the paper?
 - Any indication on how sensitive results are w.r.t. the random seed?
 - It might be a more generic criticism concerning search space design papers, but in my opinion emphasizing differences between searching for a subspace and then performing NAS, compared to performing NAS directly in the hyperspace, is often quite misleading and mostly concerns semantics rather than the core issues. For example, in the submitted paper we can read: "Constructing a huge search space to cover all devices’ preferred settings can be an intuitive solution. However, the very large search space has been demonstrated with prohibitive search cost and convergence failure issue (...) Thus, we argue that each device requires a specialized search space to achieve the optimal quantized latency-accuracy trade-off." - there is no fundamental difference between having a hyperspace from which we later search for a space and having a huge search space to cover all devices. What the submitted paper effectively does, similar to many search space design papers these days, is to propose an effective and efficient way of searching within this huge search space (hyperspace) by breaking it down into two steps. Why is it important to acknowledge that there is no fundamental difference between search space design and NAS (at least in the setting like in the submitted paper)? Because otherwise statements like "we argue that each device requires a specialized search space" would suggest that we _have to_ perform NAS in this huge search space by first searching for a subspace, but there is no evidence to support such a strong statement. Search space design methods might be the most efficient methods right now to tackle the problem of searching in large spaces like those, but we cannot guarantee they are the only sensible choice in general.
 Fundamentally, there is no difference between the objective behind standard NAS and search space design methods that utilize the concept of a hyperspace.
    
**Details:**

_W1_:

- Observation 1: in the case of FLOPs this has been showed by multiple papers by now, in the context of FP32 and INT8 it is somewhat novel but ironically the results for this part are the least convincing (only 1 devices and 2 models are shown)
- Observation 2 is common sense, it is also not unique to quantization and holds true for majority of different settings (precision, target device, etc.), there is also the problem of how latency measurements were conducted (see the last point in weaknesses)
- Observation 3: how is that different from already known facts that latency of architectures run across many devices (full precision) is weakly correlated? Specifically, the text in its current form says that the case for quantization is very different from full precision, but in my opinion that is not the case -- everything that was said in this part could have been said (and often has been already said) for full precision models
- Two-stage NAS approach is exactly the same as the one in Chen et al. "Searching the Search Space of Vision Transformer"
- Efficient approximation of Q scores (the main source of efficiency of the proposed method) and related blockwise distillation is basically tweaked DNA/DONNA, together with efficient latency estimation has been proposed in LANA
- latency prediction is done using the existing nn-Meter
- second stage NAS is basically following works like OFA, OQAT or BatchQuant (the latter overlaps quite significantly in fact).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clearly written and good quality. Novelty somewhat limited, probably impossible to reproduce without using official code (provided) considering the amount of steps, variables, and the overall complexity of the proposed method. Additionally, exactly reproducing results would require having access to the devices used by the authors in their experiments (not exactly the authors' fault).
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, I appreciate the effort put into constructing the proposed system and its strong results. Overall the submitted paper is solid with only a few notable places that would require corrections (e.g., reporting of searching time, both in the context of correcting the current numbers as well as adding end-to-end cost). However, novelty is somewhat limited, despite delivering strong results, and on top of the smaller shortcomings present throughout the paper makes it less appealing to strongly recommend the paper for acceptance. Additionally, I am a bit concerned about the excessive abuse of vspaces and the related potential problems with the final form of the paper. Because of all these issues, I would consider the paper to be borderline at this stage, however the authors should be able to convince me to increase my score with some a little bit of extra work on their paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper builds upon and extends multiple existing techniques for neural architecture search tailored for INT8 quantization. The authors propose an INT8-quantization-friendly search space, leading to higher accuracy models at near-iso-latency. The main claim of the paper is that the current methods (1) uses FLOPS as the target metric for optimization (can be misleading and it is commonly-known in the community) and (2) do not take into account the dependency between the latency of each operator and target hardware. Finally, the authors evaluate their proposed techniques across two edge devices, showing the more than 10% accuracy improvement.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

- The paper is well-written and well-motivated. Note that, some of the observations from the authors are obvious (or already presented), for example the dependency between the latency of operations and target hardware. However, I think the authors did a good job proposing a solution that further improves the existing methods in terms of model accuracy and latency. 

- The authors not only evaluate the models in terms of accuracy, but also actually deployed the model on the target hardware and measured the actual latencies.

- The comparison with the state-of-the-arts is relatively complete. Most of the compared models have been around for a while and few actually used in industry.

**Weaknesses**

- While I understand that the target goal of this paper is not the search method, but I was hoping that the authors could bring novelty in terms of search algorithm as well, instead of relying on one particular search algorithm.

- Not entirely a weakness, but as properly mentioned by the authors, extending this work beyond INT8 quantization would be an important addition for this paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
(1) If I understand correctly, you mentioned that you excluded other configuration dimensions from the search. Do you have any intuition how including such configurations changes the quality of the results (both performance and accuracy)?

(2) Along the same line, do you have any insights on the sensitivity of the quality of results with respect to configuration dimensions? Kernel size matters more or channel width?

(3) Compared to other existing methods, how long it takes to perform the search?

(4) Can you elaborate on the compilation framework? Did you enable all the optimization when evaluation the models? Could it be that one of your identified models is just a better match for compiler optimization compared to SOTA models? how different are your models compared to the most competitive models? Can you identify a particular operation(s) that is the most beneficial for the quality improvement?  

(5) (a high-level answer is sufficient) what is the main challenges to extend your proposed methods for lower bits quantization or a heterogeneous quantization for different layers?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I enjoyed reading this paper and the evaluation results was informative. In addition, I can easily see that the proposed method and the model checkpoints (if they are open-sourced by the authors) get adapted by the industry. I would like to reiterate that while the paper does not bring much novelty in terms of search algorithm, I still believe that the proposed end-to-end framework is valuable for the community.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents hardware-aware neural architecture search specifically for INT8-quantized models on Intel server CPUs (with AVX-512) and mobile CPUs (ARM-based pixel 4 snapdragon CPU). Blockwise distillation is used to build a library of block accuracies (as in prior work, DONNA [1]), and that library is then used to construct a NAS search space that yields efficient INT8 models. A family of SeqNets are found through NAS search that outperform variants from Efficientnets, FBNets, and ShuffleNets with different FLOPs budgets.


[1] Moons et al. "Distilling Optimal Neural Networks: Rapid Search in Diverse Spaces" ICCV'21
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- HW-aware NAS is important to tailor DNNs to different devices, and this paper argues that special consideration needs to be taken for INT8-quantized models.

Weaknesses:
- It is stated that FP32 latency is not well-correlated to INT8 latency. That's plausible but goes against the conventional wisdom on vector processors where a reduction in bit-width typically leads to a linear increase in SIMD size, and a linear drop in memory bandwidth requirements. Have you investigated why this is the case in your experiments?
- Something is wrong with Fig. 3 It suggests that on pixel-4 a conv1x1 with 64 channels is just as fast as a conv1x1 with half the flops (32 channels). I can confirm that this doesn't line up with my own measurements on that device. If I understand Fig. 3 correctly, it suggests that you get higher speedups with more channels monotonically. How is this possible? The SIMD size of snapdragon CPUs at 8-bit is just 16, meaning it can do a maximum 16 operations per cycle, so I would expect a sawtooth curve with period of 16 in Fig. 3. 
- Would it be possible to see your code during the review process. I am actually finding it hard to trust some of the results, but of course, I may be wrong. It would be good to see the code to either refute or confirm my concerns. It would also be good to get a sense of how optimized your code is? Some of the unexpected results may be simply because of unoptimized code. I'd be happy to increase my score if there are reasonable replies to the concerns above.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The final results improve upon the accuracy-latency tradeoff curve for Intel VNNI-capable CPUs and pixel 4 mobile phones.
The paper is generally well-written with some room for improvement in clarity, grammar etc.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I have some major concerns with this paper and I wouldn't recommend it to be considered for publication until they are addressed.

content.title: SpaceEvo: Searching Hardware-Friendly Search Space for Efficient Int8 Inference
content.TL;DR: We introduce techniques to search a quantization-friendly search space for a given device
content.abstract: INT8 quantization is an essential compression tool to deploy a deep neural network (DNN) on resource-limited edge devices. While it greatly reduces model size and memory cost, current edge-regime DNN models cannot well utilize INT8 quantization to reduce inference latency.  In this work, we find that the poor INT8 latency performance is due to the quantization-unfriendly issue: the operator and configuration (e.g., channel width) choices in a normal model design space lead to diverse quantization efficiency and can slow down the INT8 latency. To alleviate this issue, we propose SpaceEvo to efficiently search a novel hardware-aware, quantization-friendly search space, where its top-tier sub-networks achieve both superior quantization efficiency and accuracy. The key idea is to automatically evolve hardware-preferred operators and configurations guided by a search space quality metric, called Q-T score. However, naively training a candidate space from scratch for Q-T score evaluation brings prohibitive training cost, making it difficult to evolve search space on large-scale tasks (e.g., ImageNet). We further propose to conduct block-wise training and build INT8 accuracy lookup table to greatly reduce the cost. On diverse devices, SpaceEvo consistently outperforms existing manually-designed search spaces by producing both tiny and large quantized models with superior ImageNet accuracy and hardware efficiency. The discovered models, named SeqNet, achieve up to 10.1% accuracy improvement under the same latency. Our study addressed the hardware-friendly search space design challenge in NAS and paved the way for searching the search space towards efficient deployment.
